tweets: The Enclosure Acts stole 6.8 million acres of common English land and handed it to private owners. The lawyers who drafted the bills owned the land before the ink dried.
Here is the mechanism. Before enclosure, English peasants farm strips of open common land. No deed. No title. Just centuries of use. That informality is the vulnerability.

Between 1750 and 1850, Parliament passes 4,000 individual Enclosure Acts. Each one requires a private bill. Each private bill requires a solicitor. The solicitors charge £400 to £600 per act. In a county where a laborer earns £20 a year.
The commissioners appointed to survey and redistribute the land are named inside the same bills. They are paid in acreage. Not cash. Acreage. They draw their own boundary lines.
Peasants who want to contest the reallocation must file a legal objection. With a solicitor. At £600 a bill. The system prices out the only people with standing to fight it.

By 1820, 400,000 families lose access to land their ancestors farmed for 300 years. They move to the cities. They become the factory labor force that funds the Industrial Revolution. The enclosers collect rent on the land. Then buy shares in the mills the displaced workers fill.
The system that built modern England was designed by the people it made wealthy, using rules that made their wealth unchallengeable.
